title: Painting: Ajanta to the Miniature Schools

cards.h: Colour and story on walls and paper
cards.b: Painting questions in Prelims ask for school, region and theme. In Mains they ask about Mughal and Rajput contrast or Company paintings.

Bhimbetka (Madhya Pradesh), rock paintings of the Stone Age, a UNESCO site (2003). Ajanta (Maharashtra), 2nd century BCE to c. 480 CE: Buddhist cave murals. Fresco secco technique. Themes: Jataka tales, Padmapani and Vajrapani, the Mother and Child panel. Bagh caves (Madhya Pradesh). Sittanavasal (Jain, Tamil Nadu). Ellora has few paintings.

• Pala (Buddhist palm-leaf manuscripts of Nalanda, Vikramashila).
  • Jain western Indian manuscripts (Kalpasutra, Gujarat), with bold lines and large eyes, often silver and gold ink.
  • Sultanate: Persian influence, e.g. Nimatnama.
  • Vijayanagara: Lepakshi murals.

Rooted in Persian miniature. Humayun brought Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd as-Samad. Akbar: Hamzanama; Razmnama; Daswanth, Basawan. Jahangir: naturalism, portraits, birds and flowers; Ustad Mansur (falcons, flowers); Bishandas. Shah Jahan: refined, formal. Aurangzeb: court patronage fell; artists left for provincial courts. Features: realism, perspective, portraits, durbar scenes, borders.

Rajasthani (Mewar, Bundi, Kishangarh, Jaipur, Marwar): bold colours, Ragamala, Krishna Lila, Gita Govinda. Kishangarh: Bani Thani (Nihal Chand), long eyes and slender faces.

Pahari (Basohli, Guler, Kangra): soft colours, lyrical, Radha-Krishna; Kangra painting under Raja Sansar Chand, 18th century; Nainsukh of Guler. Basohli: bold and early (17th century).

• Deccani: Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmednagar; rich colours, Ragamala.
  • Company school (late 18th century): Indian artists for British patrons, with natural history subjects; Patna Kalam.
  • Raja Ravi Varma: oleo-prints, Hindu gods in realistic European style.
  • Bengal School (Abanindranath Tagore, Bharat Mata); Nandalal Bose (Constitution illustrations); Amrita Sher-Gil; Progressive Artists’ Group, 1947 (Souza, Husain, Raza).

Madhubani (Bihar, GI), Warli (Maharashtra, geometric on mud walls), Pattachitra (Odisha, West Bengal), Kalamkari (Andhra, pen work), Tanjore, Phad (Rajasthan scroll), Gond, Kalighat, Pithora, Cheriyal scrolls. Many have GI tags. Padma awards often go to these artists (e.g. Jivya Soma Mashe, Warli).

cards.h: Who gets credit: patron or painter?
cards.b: Court painting names painters rarely; the studio, karkhana, worked under a patron. Mughal paintings carried the emperor’s taste. The Bengal School turned to Asian spiritual tradition as an anti-colonial act, while Ravi Varma’s mass prints shaped popular religion. Debate: nationalism versus realism.

Madhubani on railway stations and the Warli wall art on public buildings link craft to livelihood schemes. GI tags protect makers. The National Gallery of Modern Art (Delhi, 1954) and National Museum hold masterpieces. The “One District One Product” scheme promotes such crafts.

• “Mughal and Rajput painting: similarities and differences.”
  • “Ajanta paintings in the history of Indian art.”
  • Prelims tip: Bani Thani = Kishangarh; Hamzanama = Akbar; Kangra = Pahari; Patna Kalam = Company school; Bhimbetka = prehistoric; Ajanta = fresco secco, Buddhist.
